title: C482/81/2014 of Gautam AND OTHERS Vs State Of Uttarakhand AND ANOTHER

paras.text:
Reserved on: 17.05.2019
 Delivered on: 14.06.2019
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Criminal Misc. Application No. 81 of 2014
Under Section 482 of Cr.P.C.
Gautam and others ....... Petitioners
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand & another ....Respondents
Ms. Geeta Luthra, Sr. Advocate, assisted by Mr. Sanjeev Sahay and Mr.Vipul
Sharma, Advocates for the petitioners.
Ms. Manisha Rana Singh, A.G.A. for the State.

Hon'ble Ravindra Maithani, J.
Present petition under Section 482 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as "the Code) is filed
by the petitioners for quashing the charge sheet and the entire
proceedings of Criminal Case No. 853 of 2013, under Section 3, 5, 7, 9
of Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 (hereinafter referred to as
"the Act"), pending in the court of learned Judicial Magistrate,
Ramnagar, District Nainital as well as summoning order dated
05.12.2013.
2. Heard learned senior counsel for the petitioners and
learned counsel for the State and perused the record.
3. The facts of the case, briefly stated, are that on
12.09.2013, Circle Officer, Police, Ramnagar, District Nainital upon
information having been received that in the Jungle Corbett Resort,
prostitution is being carried on, raided the resort. When the police team
reached at the resort, there was none at the reception. The police team
visited Room Nos. 201-205 of the resort and from key hole noticed
some movements in those rooms. The man and women in those rooms
were in compromising position. They were moaning and expressing the
hope that they would be deriving great pleasure soon and also that some
more customers are to come shortly. The rooms were searched, all these
four petitioners were found with the girls in the rooms. The petitioner

2
no.1 Gautam, petitioner no.2 Lalit Batra and petitioner no.3 Deepak
Kumar were with two girls each in their rooms and petitioner no.4
Pankaj Gora was with a girl. Those girls told the police team that under
pressure and being acquisitive they indulged in that activity. Some
money and other articles were recovered and a case under Sections 3, 5,
7, 9 of the Act was lodged. After investigation, charge-sheet has been
submitted against the petitioners and cognizance taken. Aggrieved,
instant petition.
4. Learned senior counsel for the petitioners would argue on
the following points:-
(i) No case under the Act has been made out against
any of the petitioners; the story is not believable at all; there is no
independent witness of the incident.
(ii) The police did not correctly disclose the identity of
the persons, whom they apprehended, because one of the girls
happens to be the wife of petitioner no.2, Lalit Batra but, she was
shown by her father's address. It is highly improbable that the
petitioner no.2 leaves his wife with some other person and would
be staying with some other woman at the same time and in the
same resort.
(iii) The resort cannot be termed as a brothel because to
term a place a brothel, a single act of prostitution is not suffice,
there should be multiple activities. Therefore, provision of
Section 3 of the Act are not attracted. In support of this, learned
senior counsel placed reliance upon the principles of law, as laid
down in the case of Suseela Vs. State 1981SCC Online Mad 199.
In the case of Suseela (supra), the Court, inter-alia, held that the
definition of 'brothel' would clearly show that 'brothel' is a
place which should be used for the purpose of prostitution for the
gain of another person or for the mutual gain of two or more
prostitutes. "For the purpose of prostitution" would undoubtedly
mean more than one instance of prostitution and solitary instance
of prostitution in a place does not make a place a brothel'.

3
(iv) There is no evidence that any of the petitioners has
either procured, induced or took any person for the sake of
prostitution. Therefore, provisions of Section 5 are also not
applicable.
(v) The provisions of Section 7 are also not applicable
in the case because there is no record to reveal, as to whether,
any area has ever been notified under this Section.
(vi) None of the girls were under the custody of any of
the petitioners, therefore, provision of Section 9 are also not
applicable.
(vii) Even if, it is assumed that petitioners were at the
resort, they may at the best be termed as customers and in that
case no provision of the Act would come into play. In support of
her contention, learned senior counsel placed reliance upon the
principles of law, as laid down in the cases of Chandru S and
another Vs. State by Malleshwaram and another [in Criminal
Petition No. 5059 of 2017, High Court of Karnataka at Bangluru
and Vivek P.B. Vs. State and another, [in Criminal Petition No.
1769 of 2018, High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru], Vinod @
Vijay Bhagubhai Patel Vs. State of Gujarat & another, 2017 SCC
Online Gujarat 446.
In the case of Vivek P.B (supra) Hon'ble High Court of
Karnataka, inter-alia, held that the person who visits brothel
house only as a customer is not covered by any of the provisions
of the Act. In the case of Chandru S (supra) and Vinod (supra)
similar proposition was held by the Hon'ble High Courts.
(viii) The mandatory provisions of Section 15 of the Act
have not been followed. In view of the fact that the provisions of
the Act have been made stringent, non compliance of Section 15
of the Act vitiates the entire proceedings. Therefore, it is argued
that it is a case where no offence is made out against the
petitioners and in exercise of its jurisdiction under Section 482 of
the Code, the proceedings deserves to be quashed and the
petition allowed.

4
5. On the other hand, learned State counsel would argue
that:-
(i) Provisions of Section 15 of the Act are directory, as
held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bai Radha Vs.
State of Gujarat 1969 (1) SCC 43. In the case of Bai Radha
(supra), the panch witnesses were not inhabitants of the locality
in which raid was conducted and it was challenged on the ground
that there was no compliance of Section 15 of the Act. Hon'ble
Supreme Court inter-alia, held as hereunder:-
"In conclusion it may be observed that the investigating
agencies cannot and ought not to show complete disregard of
such provisions as are contained in sub-sections (1) and (2) of
Section 15 of the Act. The Legislature in its wisdom provided
special safeguards owing to the nature of the premises which have
to be searched involving inroads on the privacy of citizens and
handling of delicate situations in respect of females. But the entire
proceedings and the trial do not become illegal and vitiated owing
to the non-observance of or non-compliance with the directions
contained in the aforesaid provision. The court, however, has to
be very careful and circumspect in weighing the evidence where
there has been such a failure on the part of the investigating
agency but unless and until some prejudice is shown to have been
caused to the accused person or persons the conviction and the
sentence cannot be set aside."
(ii) Even a single act may be termed a place as a
brothel. In the case of Krishnamurthy alias Tailor Krishnan, AIR
1967 SC 567, it was, inter-alia, held that it is not necessary that
there should be evidence of repeated visits by persons to the
place for the purpose of prostitution. A single instance coupled
with surrounding circumstances is sufficient to establish both
that the place was being used as a brothel and that the person
alleged was so keeping it. At this point learned senior counsel for
the petitioner responds that in the instant case there are no
surrounding circumstances.
(iii) The girls recovered from the resort have
categorically stated that they were pressurized and lured by
petitioner no.2 and one more accused namely, Vijay for the
prostitution. Moreover, it is a question of fact, which cannot be
looked into in these proceedings.

5
(iv) The officer who conducted the raid was authorized
under Section 13 of the Act.
(v) In view of the provisions of Section 7 sub-section
(2) of the Act, the petitioner no.4 Pankaj Gora, who happens to
be the Manager of the resort is liable to be punished.
(vi) The provisions of Section 9 of the Act are also
attracted because the girls are stage performers, who were
brought at the resort by the petitioner no. 2 Lalit Batra and he
pressurized, lured or abetted the girls for prostitution.
6. The facts are not much in dispute. A raid was conducted
on 12.09.2013 and the petitioners and one more person alongwith the
girls in their rooms were found in compromising positions. They were
arrested. The statements of the girls have been recorded by the
Investigating Officer, except one girl, who was found in the room of
petitioner no.3 Deepak Verma, the other girls have categorically stated
that the petitioner no.2 Lalit Batra pressurized them for prostitution.
7. Though in these proceedings some affidavits have been
filed on behalf of the petitioners and affidavit of the girls and others but
these documents cannot be looked into to appreciate the arguments.
This is not a trial.
8. In these proceedings under Section 482 of the Code,
interference is not easily made. In the case of State of Haryana and
Others Vs. Bhajan Lal and Others, 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335, Hon'ble
Supreme Court has laid down the test for exercising the inherent power
of the High Court under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
It was held that :-
"102. In the backdrop of the interpretation of the various
relevant provisions of the Code under Chapter XIV and of the
principles of law enunciated by this Court in a series of decisions
relating to the exercise of the extraordinary power under Article
226 or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code which
we have extracted and reproduced above, we give the following
categories of cases by way of illustration wherein such power
could be exercised either to prevent abuse of the process of any
court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, though it may not
be possible to lay down any precise, clearly defined and

6
sufficiently channelised and inflexible guidelines or rigid
formulae and to give an exhaustive list of myriad kinds of cases
wherein such power should be exercised.
(1) Where the allegations made in the first information
report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value
and accepted in their entirety do not prima facie constitute any
offence or make out a case against the accused.
(2) Where the allegations in the first information report
and other materials, if any, accompanying the FIR do not disclose
a cognizable offence, justifying an investigation by police officers
under Section 156(1) of the Code except under an order of a
Magistrate within the purview of Section 155(2) of the Code.
(3) Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR
or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do
not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case
against the accused.
(4) Where, the allegations in the FIR do not constitute a
cognizable offence but constitute only a non-cognizable offence,
no investigation is permitted by a police officer without an order
of a Magistrate as contemplated under Section 155(2) of the
Code.
(5) Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint
are so absurd and inherently improbable on the basis of which no
prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is
sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.
(6) Where there is an express legal bar engrafted in any of
the provisions of the Code or the concerned Act (under which a
criminal proceeding is instituted) to the institution and
continuance of the proceedings and/or where there is a specific
provision in the Code or the concerned Act, providing efficacious
redress for the grievance of the aggrieved party.
(7) Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended
with mala fide and/or where the proceeding is maliciously
instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance on the
accused and with a view to spite him due to private and personal
grudge.
103. We also give a note of caution to the effect that the
power of quashing a criminal proceeding should be exercised
very sparingly and with circumspection and that too in the rarest
of rare cases; that the court will not be justified in embarking
upon an enquiry as to the reliability or genuineness or otherwise
of the allegations made in the FIR or the complaint and that the
extraordinary or inherent powers do not confer an arbitrary
jurisdiction on the court to act according to its whim or caprice."
(emphasis supplied)
9. Arguments have been advanced with regard to the
improbability of the story. In the cases of direct evidence, as the instant
one, appreciation at this stage may not be done, on the basis of
probability of the story.
10. Insofar as disclosure of correct identity is concerned, it's
again a matter of fact. Prosecution case is specific that the petitioners
were found with girls in compromising position, moaning etc. Whether

7
any of the girls was wife of the petitioner no.2 or not, and if so, it's
effect? It's again a matter of evidence.
11. Petitioners have been summoned under Section 3 of the
Act. Section 3 of the Act provides punishment for keeping a brothel or
allowing premises to be used as a brothel. Before arguments in this
context are appreciated, it would be expedient to see as to what brothel
means. Brothel has been defined under Section 2 (a) of the Act, which
is as hereunder:
"(a) "brothel" includes any house room, conveyance or
place or any portion of any house, room, conveyance or place,
which is used for purposes of sexual exploitation or abuse for the
gain of another person or for the mutual gain of two or more
prostitutes."
12. In the case of Suseela (supra), it is categorically held that
to term a place as brothel, there should be more than one instance of
prostitution. In the case of Krishnamurthy alias Tailor Krishnan
(supra), Hon'ble Supreme Court has held that single instance coupled
with surrounding circumstances is sufficient to establish a place as a
brothel. In that case, surrounding circumstances were that a decoy was
sent, who was shown three girls and he paid for one. Those
circumstances were weighed and considered as surrounding
circumstances to establish that the place is a brothel. In the instant case,
the case of the prosecution is that, the girls were brought from Delhi
and at that resort they were seduced for prostitution. This is one single
act. There are no other surrounding circumstances, which may indicate
that the place was really being used for the purpose of prostitution,
therefore, it appears that offence under Section 3 of the Act is not prima
facie made out in the case.
13. On behalf of the petitioners reference has been made to
para 6 of the judgment in the case of Dilip Varghese Vs. State of Kerala
(Crl. M.C. 930 of 2011) to indicate that it is not a case of prosecution.
In the case of Dilip Varghese (supra), in para 5 of the judgment
applicability of Section 7 of the Act was discussed, particularly, in view
of definition of "prostitution" under Section 2 (f) of the Act. In para 6,
it was observed that prosecution has no case that petitioners had

8
indulged in sexual intercourse. In that case, while holding that there
was no evidence of sexual intercourse, much less prostitution or
carrying on prostitution and proceedings of that case was quashed. No
doubt to invoke the provisions of Section 7 (1) of the Act, it should be
an act in continuity because words used is "carries on prostitution". But
here is a case where according to the prosecution, the girls recovered
from the resort were lured and pressurized for prostitution. What is
prostitution? Is it necessarily sexual intercourse? Should it be
necessarily sexual intercourse with different persons? In the case of
Gaurav Jain Vs. Union of India and others (1997) 8 SCC 114, Honble
Supreme Court observed as hereunder:
"19. Therefore, prostitution is not confined, as in the
ITP Act, to offering of the body to a person for promiscuous
sexual intercourse. Normally, the word "prostitution" means an
act of promiscuous sexual intercourse for hire or offer or
agreement to perform an act of sexual intercourse or any unlawful
sexual act for hire as was the connotation of the Act. By
amendment the act of a female and exploitation of her person by
an action or process of exploitation for commercial purpose
making use of or working up for exploitation of the person of the
women taking unjust and unlawful advantage of trapped women
for one's benefit or sexual intercourse has been brought within its
frame. The word "abuse" has a very wide meaning - every thing
which is contrary to good order established by usage amounts to
abuse. Physical or mental maltreatment also is an
abuse.................."
14. The definition of prostitution under Section 2 (f) of the
Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956 may be
referred, which is as hereunder:
 "prostitution" means the act of a female offering her body for
promiscuous sexual intercourse for hire, whether in money or in
kind."
In the year 1978, the definition of prostitution was
substituted as hereunder:-
"prostitution" means the act of a female offering her body for
promiscuous sexual intercourse for hire, whether in money or in
kind, and whether offered immediately or otherwise, and the
expression "prostitute" shall be construed accordingly."
And, finally this definition was further changed,
which is as hereunder:-

9
"prostitution" means the sexual exploitation or abuse of
persons for commercial purposes, and the expression "prostitute"
shall be construed accordingly.
15. The above evaluation of the definition of prostitution in
view of the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Gaurav Jain's case
(supra) makes it abundantly clear that for prostitution promiscuous
sexual intercourse is not an essential factor. It is simply "sexual
exploitation or abuse of persons for commercial purposes. The abuse, as
has been defined in Gaurav Jain case (supra) means everything which
is contrary to good order established by usage amounts to abuse.
Therefore, principle of law as laid down in the case of Dilip Varghese
(supra) may not be applicable in view of Gaurav Jain's case (supra).
16. It is true that in the cases of Vivek P.B. (supra) and
Chandru S. (supra), Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka has held that if
the customer visits a brothel, he will not be held liable under any
provision of the Act. A bare perusal of the provisions, makes it clear
that a person, who simply visits the prostitutes cannot be said to have
committed any offence under the Act, unless he does some other act,
which may bring him under some specific provisions of the Act e.g.
Sections 5, 7 & 9 etc. of the Act.
17. Arguments have been advanced on behalf of the petitioner
that in the instant case, compliance of Section 15 of the Act has not
been made and it vitiates the entire proceedings. It is argued that since
the provisions of the Act are stringent, therefore, requirement of the
provisions should be strictly followed and it should be considered as
mandatory. Reference has been made to Section 50 of the Narcotic
Drugs and Psychotropic Act, 1985 (hereinafter referred to as "the
N.D.P.S. Act). To argue that since provisions of N.D.P.S. Act are
stringent, therefore, compliance of Section 50 of the Act, repeatedly has
been held mandatory by the Hon'ble Supreme Court. Reliance has been
placed to the judgments of State of Rajasthan Vs. Parmanand and
another (2014) 5 SCC 345 and Dilip and another Vs. State of Madhya
Pradesh (2007) 1 SCC 450. In the cases of Dilip and Parmanand
(supra) Hon'ble Court, inter alia, held that compliance of Section 50 of
the N.D.P.S. Act is mandatory.

10
18. Learned senior counsel for the petitioner has also
distinguished the case of Bai Radha (supra), on the ground that in that
case though, compliance of Section 15 of the Act was made but, it was
not complete, as panch witnesses were not local. Therefore, it is argued
that whatever observations have been made by the Hon'ble Supreme
Court with regard to Section 15 of the Act, in the case of Bai Radha
(supra) will not be applicable because in the instant case compliance of
Section 15 of the Act has at all not been made.
Section 15 of the Act reads as hereunder:
15. Search without warrant.-(1) Notwithstanding
anything contained in any other law for the time being in force,
whenever the special police officer or the trafficking police
officer, as the case may be, has reasonable grounds for believing
that an offence punishable under this Act has been or is being
committed in respect of a person living in any premises, and that
search of the premises with warrant cannot be made without
undue delay, such officer may, after recording the grounds of his
belief, enter and search such premises without a warrant.
(2) Before making a search under sub-section (1), the
special police officer or the trafficking police officer, as the case
may be, shall call upon two or more respectable inhabitants at
least one of whom shall be a woman of the locality in which the
place to be searched is situate, to attend and witness the search,
and may issue an order in writing to them or any of them so to do:
Provided that the requirement as to the respectable
inhabitants being from the locality in which the place to be
searched is situate shall not apply to a woman required to attend
and witness the search.
(3) Any person who, without reasonable cause, refuses or
neglects, to attend and witness a search under this section, when
called upon to do so by an order in writing delivered or tendered
to him, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under
section 187 of the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860).
(4) The special police officer or the trafficking police
officer, as the case may be, entering any premises under sub-section (1) shall be entitled to remove therefrom all the persons
found therein.
(5) The special police officer or the trafficking police
officer, as the case may be, after removing the person under sub-section (4) shall forthwith produce him before the appropriate
magistrate.
(5A) Any person who is produced before a magistrate
under sub-section (5), shall be examined by a registered medical
practitioner for the purposes of determination of the age of such
person, or for the detection of any injuries as a result of sexual
abuse or for the presence of any sexually transmitted diseases.
Explanation.-In this sub-section, "registered medical
practitioner" has the same meaning as in the Indian Medical
Council Act, 1956 (102 of 1956).
(6) The special police officer or the trafficking police
officer, as the case may be, and other persons taking part in, or

11
attending, and witnessing a search shall not be liable to any civil
or criminal proceedings against them in respect of anything
lawfully done in connection with, or for the purpose of, the
search.
(6A) The special police officer or the trafficking police
officer, as the case may be, making a search under this section
shall be accompanied by at least two women police officers, and
where any woman or girl removed under sub-section (4) is
required to be interrogated, it shall be done by a woman police
officer and if no woman police officer is available, the
interrogation shall be done only in the presence of a lady member
of a recognised welfare institution or organisation.
Explanation.-For the purpose of this sub-section and
section 17A, "recognised welfare institution or organisation"
means such institution or organisation as may be recognised in
this behalf by the State Government.
(7) The provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure,
1973 (2 of 1974), shall, so far as may be, apply to any search
under this section as they apply to any search made under the
authority of a warrant issued under section 94 of the said Code.
19. Bare perusal of the above, reveals that before making a
search, two or more respectable inhabitants, at least one of whom shall
be a woman should be invited to join search and witness it. In the
instant case, compliance of Section 15 of the Act is not at all made.
20. In the case of Bai Radha (supra), Hon'ble Supreme Court,
inter alia, held that entire proceedings of the trial do not become illegal
and vitiated owing to the non-observance of or non-compliance with the
direction contained in Section 15 of the Act. However, Hon'ble Court
has cautioned that when such compliance is not made, the Court has to
be very careful and circumspect in weighing the evidence, where there
has been such a failure on the part of the investigating agency.
Therefore, in view of the law, as laid down in the case of Bai Radha
(supra) non-compliance of Section 15 of the Act does not make a
ground for interference under Section 482 of the Code. [See Also
R.A.H. Siguran Vs. Shankare Gowda @ Shankara and another, (2017)
16 SCC 126]
21. The girls recovered from the room of the petitioner no.1
have stated that they visited the resort at the instance of petitioner No.2
Lalit Batra. And the girls recovered from the rooms of the petitioners

12
told it to the Investigating Officer that under pressure of Mr. Lalit Batra
and petitioner no.4 Pankaj Gora and being acquisitive, they committed
the mistake. One of them has categorically stated that she was
pressurized for it by the petitioner no.2. The girls recovered from the
room of petitioner no.2 Lalit Batra have also stated that under pressure
they did the act. Other girls have also stated about it. One of the girls
has also named co-accused Vijay.
22. According to the prosecution case, these girls were
brought from Delhi on the pretext of some stage performance. They
were stage artists and were lured with money and pressurized for
prostitution, as they have stated. Petitioner no.2 brought the girls at the
resorts, therefore, he definitely had a position of authority over these
girls. It may be temporary. Apparently, it will, prima facie, attract
provisions of Sections 5 and 9 of the Act against the petitioner no.2
Lalit Batra, who allegedly lured those girls and pressurized them for
prostitution. Petitioner no.4 being a Manager of the resort has permitted
the resort to be used for prostitution. He according to the recovered
girls also pressurized them for prostitution. Therefore, apparently
provisions of Sections 5 & 7 (2) of the Act, prima facie, attracts against
the petitioner no.4. In these proceedings, much of the discussion of the
evidence is not required.
23. As discussed hereinbefore, in the instant case, prima facie,
no case is made out against the petitioner no.1 Gautam and petitioner
no.3 Deepak Verma. But, a case under Sections 5 and 9 of the Act is,
prima facie, made out against the petitioner no.2 Lalit Batra and a case
under Sections 5 and 7 (2) of the Act is, prima facie, made out against
petitioner no.4 Pankaj Gora. Therefore, insofar as, the petitioner no.1
Gautam and petitioner no.3 Deepak Verma is concerned, an
interference is warranted and proceedings against them may be
quashed. But, insofar as, petitioner no.2 Lalit Batra and petitioner no.4
Pankaj Gora are concerned, no interference is warranted.
24. The petition is partly allowed. Proceedings of Criminal
Case No. 853 of 2013, under Section 3, 5, 7, 9 of the Act, pending in

13
the court of learned Judicial Magistrate, Ramnagar, District Nainital is
quashed qua petitioner no.1 Gautam & petitioner no.3 Deepak Verma.
25. Prima facie, offence under Section 5 & 9 of the Act is
made out against petitioner no.2 Lalit Batra and prima facie, offence
under Sections 5 and 7 (2) of the Act is made out against the petitioner
no.4 Pankaj Gora. Therefore, in respect of the petitioner no.2 Lalit
Batra and petitioner no.4 Pankaj Gora, no interference is warranted &
the case shall proceed against them.
(Ravindra Maithani, J.)
 Jitendra
